Do women, children and the aged in your house not grieve or beg? Are the kinswomen honoured in your house, bull among men?
mahabharata:15:33.9	Does this line of royal sages, having reached such a king, great king, not decline in fame as is fit?
mahabharata:15:33.13	Does he not always blame us as wrongdoers for the sons slain, of great valour, devoted to kshatriya dharma?
mahabharata:15:33.14	And where is Vidura, king? We do not see him. And is Sanjaya well, and standing in austerity?
Thus addressed, Dhritarashtra replied to the lord of men: "Vidura is well, son, and has taken up terrible austerity.
Living on air, without food, thin, his veins showing, he is sometimes seen by brahmins somewhere in this empty forest."
As he was saying this, Kshatta was seen from afar by the king's guards: matted-haired, with a pebble in his mouth, thin, naked, his limbs smeared with dirt, covered with forest dust.
Turning back suddenly, seeing the people toward the hermitage, he was pointed out to the king.
Yudhishthira alone ran after him as he entered the terrible forest, seen and unseen here and there.
O Vidura, I am the king, Yudhishthira, dear to you! the king said as he ran after him with effort.
Then in a lonely, secluded spot, the best of the wise, Vidura, stood leaning on a tree somewhere in the forest.
The greatly wise king Yudhishthira recognised the greatly wise one, mostly wasted, made known only by his form.
Saying "I am Yudhishthira," he stood before him, and the king made it heard by Vidura, and he answered by sign.
Then, becoming unblinking, he looked at the king, fixing his gaze on him with his gaze, composed.
The wise Vidura entered him, limbs into limbs, placing breath in breath and senses in senses.
Relying on the power of yoga, Vidura entered the body of the king of dharma, blazing as it were with radiance.
Then the king saw Vidura's body, stiff-eyed, as it was, leaning on the tree, its consciousness gone.
The greatly radiant king of dharma thought himself strong, with many qualities, and remembered that.
The learned one, lord of the people, remembered all that was ancient to himself, the yoga dharma as told by Vyasa.
The king of dharma then wished to have the body cremated there, and wished to burn it; then a voice spoke.

O king, this body called Vidura is not to be burned; this is your dharma, the eternal dharma.
mahabharata:15:33.32	He will have the worlds called Santanaka, king; he has gained the dharma of an ascetic and is not to be grieved for, scourge of foes.
Thus addressed, the king of dharma turned back and told Vichitravirya's son all that.
Then that radiant king and all the people, and Bhimasena and the rest, came to great amazement.
Hearing it, the king, pleased, said to the son of Dharma: "Take this water, root and fruit of mine.
As a man eats, king, so the guest is held to eat." So told, Dharma's son said "So be it" to the king, and with his brothers ate the fruit and roots given by the king.
Then they, having taken their dwellings at the roots of trees, spent that night eating fruit, roots and water.
There were tales there among them marked by dharma and wealth, moving in varied words and joined with many traditions.
The Pandavas slept on the ground all round their mother then, king, leaving very costly beds.
What food King Dhritarashtra, the great-minded, had, the same food the kings lived on that night.
When the night had passed and they had done their forenoon rites, Kunti's son with his brothers saw the circle of hermitages,
with the women's quarters, followers and priest, as they liked and wherever they wished, with Dhritarashtra's leave.
There he saw altars with blazing fires, attended by sages who had bathed and offered into the fires.
They were adorned with heaps of wild flowers, with rising smoke of ghee, of Brahmic form and crowded with hosts of sages.
Unalarmed herds of deer rested there and there, and flocks of birds, unafraid, as if singing, lord.
In places it was adorned with the sound of recited Vedas and richly beautified with great loads of fruit and roots.
Then the king gave for the ascetics golden pitchers that had been brought, and also udumbara ones, O king.
Deer-skins, braids, ladles and spoons, water-pots, dishes and pots, O Bharata, the king gave.
Iron vessels and varied dishes, king, whatever they wished and as much, and whatever else they desired.
So that righteous king, out of love for the circle of hermitages, gave away all that wealth and came back again.
He saw the wise King Dhritarashtra, who had done his daily rites, sitting unflustered with Gandhari.
And the righteous one saw his mother standing not far off, bowed like a pupil, Kunti, always practising dharma.
He honoured the king, announced his own name, and, told "Sit," sat on a seat of grass.
Bhimasena and the other Pandavas, having saluted and embraced the best of the Kauravas, sat by the king's command.
Surrounded by them, that Kaurava king shone greatly, bearing Brahmic glory, like Brihaspati with the gods.
As they sat, the great sages who lived at Kurukshetra, Shatayupa and the others, gathered.
And the blessed brahmin Vyasa, honoured by hosts of divine sages, surrounded by pupils, of great radiance, appeared to the king.
Then the Kaurava king, and Kunti's mighty son, and Bhimasena and the others rose and honoured him.
Vyasa, having come, surrounded by Shatayupa and the others, said to King Dhritarashtra, "Be seated."
Then Vyasa took the new seat of kusha, with black deer-skin and kusha grass over it, prepared for that purpose.
And all those best of brahmins of great radiance sat on seats on all sides, permitted by Dvaipayana.
[Vyasa] "Mighty-armed Dhritarashtra, does your austerity grow? Is your mind pleased in forest life, lord of men?
Is there no grief in your heart for the slaying of your sons, king? Are all your knowledges serene, blameless one?
Having made your mind firm, do you follow the forest rule? And your wife Gandhari, is she not overcome by grief?
Is this goddess of great wisdom, intelligent, seeing dharma and wealth, knowing the truth of tradition and departure, not grieving?
And Kunti, king, who serves you without pride, who gave up her kingdom to serve her elders?
Is the king of dharma, your son, welcomed by you with love, and Bhima, Arjuna and the twins, are they comforted?
Are you glad seeing them? Is your mind stainless? Are you of pure feeling, king, with knowledge born?
These three are the best among all beings, Bharata: freedom from enmity, truth and non-malice, great king.
And I know, king, the departure of the great-souled Vidura by the rule by which the very great soul of Dharma went.
By Mandavya's curse Dharma went to the state of Vidura: greatly wise, a great yogi, great-souled, of great mind.
Neither Brihaspati among the gods nor Shukra among the asuras was so endowed with wisdom as that bull among men.
Having spent a vast store of austerity gathered long, eternal Dharma was overcome by the sage Mandavya.
At Brahma's command, long ago, by my own strength, that very wise one was born in Vichitravirya's field.
Your brother, great king, the god of gods, eternal, whom the sages know as dharma by upholding the good and meditation,
increases by truth, self-control, observance, non-harm, giving and austerity, the eternal one.
By whose power of yoga the Kuru king Yudhishthira was born, he, king, is called Dharma by the wise of immeasurable wisdom.
As fire, wind, water, earth and space stand, so dharma stands here and hereafter.
All-pervading, Kaurava, pervading all moving and unmoving, the god of gods is seen by perfected ones whose sins are burned away.
He who is dharma is Vidura; he who is Vidura is the Pandava; this Pandava is in your control, standing like a servant, king.
Your wise brother has entered his own self, by good fortune, the great soul, endowed with great yoga power, into Kunti's son.
I too shall soon join you to the good, bull of the Bharatas; know that I have come, son, to cut your doubt.
What was never done before in the world by any great sages, I shall show you, the marvel that is the fruit of austerity.
What do you wish to obtain from me, king, beyond the human: to see, touch or hear? Say, and I shall do it so."
[Janamejaya] "When Vidura was perfected and took refuge in the king of dharma, and all the Pandavas were staying in the circle of hermitages,
that marvel which Vyasa, greatly radiant sage, said he would do: tell me about that.
And how long did the Kaurava Yudhishthira, the unfallen king, stay in the forest with his people, brahmin?
What did they eat there, lord, staying with the army and the women's quarters, great souls? Tell me that, blameless one."
[Vaishampayana] "Given leave then by the king of the Kurus, the Pandavas rested and enjoyed various foods and drinks.
For a month they sported in the forest with the army and the women's quarters; then Vyasa came as I told you, blameless one.
So with the tales of all those in the king's presence, they attended Vyasa, O king, and other sages came.
Narada, Parvata, the greatly ascetic Devala, Vishvavasu, Tumburu and Chitrasena, O Bharata.
They sat down, having received honour from Yudhishthira, on holy seats of excellent kusha grass.
When they were seated, the greatly wise king, upholder of the Kurus, sat, surrounded by the Pandavas.
Gandhari, Kunti, Draupadi, the Satvati and the other women sat down with the other women.
Divine and righteous tales were told there, king, of ancient sages, mixed with gods and asuras.
Then at the end of the tales Vyasa, best of speakers, the greatly radiant best of Veda-knowers, pleased, said again this to the lord with wisdom as eyes:

It is known to me, king of kings, what is in your heart to say, you burned by grief made by your son.
mahabharata:15:36.17	And what grief stays in Gandhari's heart, king, and what, great king, in Kunti's and Draupadi's hearts,
mahabharata:15:36.18	and the intense sorrow Subhadra, Krishna's sister, bears from the loss of her son: that too is known to me.
mahabharata:15:36.19	Hearing this meeting of you all, I came, king, to cut your doubts, delight of the Kurus.
mahabharata:15:36.20	Let these gods, gandharvas and all the great sages see today the power of my long-gathered austerity.
mahabharata:15:36.21	So tell me, mighty-armed one, what wish I shall grant you; I am ready to give a boon; see the strength of my austerity.
Thus addressed by Vyasa of immeasurable wisdom, the king, after reflecting a moment, began to speak.
[Dhritarashtra] "I am blessed and favoured, my life is fruitful, since I meet today here with you good ones.
Today I know the goal desired for myself, since I am united with you, equal to Brahma, ascetics.
By seeing you alone I am purified, without doubt; I have no fear of the next world, blameless ones.
But my mind is always grieved, remembering that very ill-minded fool, greedy for sons, whose wrongs were great.
By whom the blameless Pandavas were wronged, sinful of mind, and this earth was suddenly slain with men and elephants.
And the great-souled kings, lords of varied lands, having come for my son's sake, all fell under death's control.
Those heroes who gave up sons, wives and dear lives and went to the house of the king of the dead,
what is their goal, brahmin, who were slain in battle for a friend's sake, and those of my sons and grandsons killed in the fight?
My mind is constantly pained for having had the mighty Bhishma, Shantanu's aged son, and Drona the best of brahmins killed.
By my foolish, sinful son, hater of friends, a blazing family was brought to destruction, he who wished the earth's kingdom.
Remembering all this, burning day and night, struck by grief and sorrow, I find no peace; as I think so, father, I have no comfort."
[Vaishampayana] Of Kunti, Drupada's daughter, Subhadra, and the other fair women, the Kaurava's daughters-in-law,
Gandhari, struck by grief for her sons, with eyes bound, rose with folded hands and said this to her father-in-law:

Sixteen years have passed, best of sages; for this king grieving for his slain sons there is no peace, lord.
mahabharata:15:37.5	Filled with grief for his sons, sighing, this king Dhritarashtra, great sage, does not sleep through all the nights.
mahabharata:15:37.6	You are able to create other worlds by the power of austerity; how much more to show the king his sons gone to other worlds?
mahabharata:15:37.7	And this Krishna Draupadi, her kin and sons slain, grieves greatly, your good daughter, the dearest of your daughters-in-law.
mahabharata:15:37.8	So too Krishna's sister Subhadra, of good speech, tormented by her son Saubhadra's slaying, grieves greatly, the lovely one.
mahabharata:15:37.9	And this wife of Bhurishravas, in the greatest sorrow, afflicted by grief at her husband's calamity, does not sleep through the nights, lord.
mahabharata:15:37.11	And the glorious hundred sons of your wise, never-fleeing son, slain at the head of battle,
mahabharata:15:37.12	their hundred wives, struck by grief for their sons, increasing again and again the king's grief and mine, with great effort wait on me, great sage.
mahabharata:15:37.13	And those heroes, great-souled great chariot-fighters, my fathers-in-law, Somadatta and the rest: what is their goal, lord?
mahabharata:15:37.14	By your grace, blessed one, may this king be free of sorrow, so that I might die, and Kunti, and your daughter-in-law here.
When Gandhari had spoken, Kunti, her face thin with vows, remembered her son born secretly, born of the Sun.
The sage, boon-giver, Vyasa, of far hearing and sight, saw her grieved, the goddess mother of Savyasachin.
Vyasa said to her: "What you wish to say, great one, tell it, whatever is in your mind."
Then Kunti, bowing her head to her parents-in-law, said with shame, revealing the old matter:
The ascetic, wrathful brahmin named Durvasa came to my father's house for alms to eat, and I satisfied him.
By purity, by giving up offences and with a pure mind, I never grew angry even at things greatly provoking anger.
Pleased, he gave me a boon; I said, "It is done"; he said to me, "You must accept it."
Then from fear of a curse I again said to the brahmin, "So be it"; and the twice-born said again to me:
You will be the mother of Dharma, fair one, lovely-faced; the gods you invoke will come under your control.
Having said this, the brahmin vanished, and I was amazed; and in all states my memory did not perish.
Then, standing on the palace roof, looking at the rising sun, remembering the sage's words, longing for the sun, I, in childishness, did not see the fault.
Then the thousand-rayed god came near me, dividing his body in two, on earth and in the sky; with one he heated the worlds, with the second he came to me.
He said to me, trembling, "Choose a boon from me; go"; and I, bowing my head, said to him:
The sharp-rayed one said, "Your summoning cannot be in vain; I shall burn you and the brahmin who gave you the boon."
Protecting the blameless brahmin from the curse, I then said, "Let me have a son like you, god."
Then the radiant one, entering me with splendour and bewildering me, said, "You will have a son," and went to heaven.
Then in my father's house, guarding the secret, I cast into the water the boy Karna, the son born secretly.
Surely by that god's favour I again became a maiden, brahmin, as the sage told me.
I, bewildered, neglected that son though knowing him; that burns me, brahmin sage, as it is well known to you.
Whether sin or no sin, this has been disclosed by me; you, blessed one, should remove this fear of mine.
And what is in this king's heart, known to you, blameless one, let him gain that wish today itself, best of sages."
Thus addressed, Vyasa, best of Veda-knowers, replied: "Good; all this is true, as you say to me.
There is no offence in you; you were in a maiden state, and gods of lordship enter bodies.
There are classes of gods who produce resolves in five ways: by word, by sight, by touch, by contact, and so.
Human dharma is not joined to divine dharma; know this, Kunti; let the fever of your mind go.
All is wholesome for the mighty, all is pure for the mighty, all is dharma for the mighty, all is their own for the mighty."

Kunti will see Karna, and the Yadava woman her son Saubhadra, Draupadi her five sons, fathers and brothers too.
mahabharata:15:39.3	This resolve was in my heart from before, as I was urged by the king, by you, and by Pritha herself.
mahabharata:15:39.4	Those great souls, all bulls among men, are not to be grieved for; devoted to kshatriya dharma, they met their end so.
mahabharata:15:39.5	That was surely to be, blameless one, the work of the gods; so all of them came down to earth in portions of gods.
mahabharata:15:39.6	Gandharvas, apsarases, pishachas, guhyakas, rakshasas, punyajanas, perfected ones and divine sages,
mahabharata:15:39.7	gods, danavas and stainless brahmin sages: these met their end at Kurukshetra in battle.
mahabharata:15:39.8	The wise king of the gandharvas called Dhritarashtra is the same Dhritarashtra in the human world, your husband.
mahabharata:15:39.9	Know Pandu as the Maruts, the most excellent, the unfallen; Kshatta was a portion of Dharma, and this King Yudhishthira too.
mahabharata:15:39.11	Know Bhimasena, the strong scourge of foes, as from the Maruts; know Arjuna, Partha, Dhananjaya as Nara the sage; Narayana as Hrishikesha, and the twins as the Ashvins.
mahabharata:15:39.12	Dividing his body, the Sun, best by austerity, heating the worlds: know that as Karna, fair one, who arose for enmity and brought on conflict.
mahabharata:15:39.13	And the Pandava heir slain by six great chariot-fighters, that Soma became here Saubhadra, who by yoga was made two.
mahabharata:15:39.14	Know Dhrishtadyumna, born with Draupadi, as a fair portion of Fire from the fire, and Shikhandin a rakshasa.
mahabharata:15:39.15	Know Drona as Brihaspati's portion and Drona's son as born of Rudra; and know Bhishma, Ganga's son, as a Vasu who came to human state.
mahabharata:15:39.16	So these gods, greatly wise one, came to human state and, having done fair deeds, went back to heaven.
mahabharata:15:39.17	And the sorrow which has long stayed in all your hearts, I shall remove today from fear of the next world.
mahabharata:15:39.18	Let all of you go to the river Bhagirathi; there you will see all those who were slain in this battle.
[Vaishampayana] Hearing Vyasa's word, all the people then went toward the Ganga with a great lion's roar.
Dhritarashtra with his ministers set out with the Pandavas, together with the tigers among sages and the gandharvas who had come.
Then, reaching the Ganga in order, the ocean of people all made camp as they pleased and as was easy.
The wise king too, with the Pandavas, with his followers, made camp in a chosen place, with women and elders first.
That day seemed to them like a hundred years as they waited for night, wishing to see the slain kings.
Then the sun reached the holy best of mountains, the setting one; then, having bathed, they did the night's rites.
Dhritarashtra, the righteous, with the Pandavas, pure and single-minded, sat with those sages.
The women sat together with Gandhari, and the townspeople and country people, all by age.
Then the greatly radiant, great sage Vyasa, plunging into the holy waters of the Bhagirathi, called all the worlds.
The Pandavas' warriors and all of the Kauravas, and the greatly fortunate kings dwelling in various lands.
Then, Janamejaya, a very tumultuous sound arose among the people, as before from the Kuru and Pandava armies.
Then all those kings, with Bhishma and Drona before them, with their armies, rose from that water by thousands.
Both Virata and Drupada with sons and soldiers, the sons of Draupadi, Saubhadra, and the rakshasa Ghatotkacha,
both Karna and Duryodhana, and the great chariot-fighter Shakuni, and Duhshasana and the other great chariot-fighter sons of Dhritarashtra.
These and many others, not named because of their number, all of shining bodies, rose then from the water.
Whatever hero's dress, banner and vehicle, so each of those kings was seen with them.
All wore divine garments and all bright earrings, free of enmity and ego, without anger or wrath.
Sung to by gandharvas and praised by bards, wearing divine garlands and garments, surrounded by hosts of apsarases,
the sage, Satyavati's son, pleased, then gave Dhritarashtra divine sight by his austerity, king.
The renowned Gandhari too, endowed with the power of divine knowledge, saw all those sons and others slain in the battle.
That marvellous, inconceivable, very great, hair-raising sight was seen by all the people, amazed, with unblinking eyes.
That force, its festival high with exultation, crowded with glad men and women, was seen coming like a picture on cloth.
Seeing them all with divine sight, Dhritarashtra rejoiced, best of the Bharatas, by that sage's grace.
Resorting to the supreme rule, fair and set by the brahmin sage, all were glad in mind, like immortals in the world of the gods.
Son met father and mother, wife met husband, brother met brother, friend met friend, king.
The Pandavas with joy came together with the great archer Karna and Saubhadra and all the sons of Draupadi.
Then, pleased, the Pandavas, meeting Karna, came to be kings in friendship.
By the sage's favour those other kshatriyas too, their anger lost, giving up enmity, stood in friendship.
So all those tigers among men, Kurus and other men, met with elders, kinsmen and sons.
Having sported that whole night, glad in mind, those kings thought themselves, in contentment, like those in heaven's assembly.
There was no grief, fear, dread, discontent or disgrace as the warriors met one another, best of the Bharatas.
The great souls, having plunged into the holy river of three paths, with their chariots and banners went to their own places.
Some went to the world of the gods, some to Brahma's assembly, some gained the world of Varuna, some Kubera's.
Some kings gained the world of Vaivasvata, some of rakshasas and pishachas, some the northern Kurus.
Of varied goals, all those great souls, gained with the immortals, went with their svaha-offerings and followers.
When they had all gone, the great sage standing in the water, righteous and greatly radiant, ever doing good to the Kurus, then said to all the kshatriya women whose lords were slain:
Whatever best women wish for the worlds made by their husbands, let them quickly plunge into the Jahnavi's water, tirelessly.
Then, hearing his words, those fair women, faithful, took leave of their father-in-law and entered the Jahnavi's water.
Freed from human bodies, then those good women all met their husbands together, lord of the people.
So in order all those virtuous high-born women, entering the water and freed, went to the same world as their husbands.
Endowed with divine form, adorned with divine ornaments, wearing divine garlands and garments, they were like their husbands.
Having said this, the hero Arjuna entered the Sudharma assembly hall of the Yadavas, grieving for the great chariot-fighters.
Spreading the fame of the great-souled Pandavas in the world, and of other kshatriyas of great wealth and splendour.
